# Omni View Central & South America
> **Sixty million reais yielded about two hundred fifty thousand votes and no Chamber seats for Cidadania.**

**What You Need to Know:** Cidadania took about two hundred fifty thousand votes after sixty million reais in public campaign money and won no seats in Brazil’s Chamber of Deputies. Elsewhere, marchers in Chubut protested a move to open Argentine land and natural resources to foreign owners, and Niterói opens a national power-soccer championship. Uruguay’s president says friendship with Lula will not set relations with Brazil after the October 25 runoff.

### Lead
**Cidadania caminha para desaparecer do mapa político nacional: O Globo**
After a run of court fights over who commands the party, Cidadania reached the end of the first round of Brazil’s 2026 elections in steep decline, O Globo reports. Federated with the PSDB, the party began as the PCB, became the PPS, and later took the name Cidadania as it moved away from its communist origins. It received 60 million reais from the Electoral Fund and gathered only about 250,000 votes nationwide. It elected one candidate to a state assembly and none to the Chamber of Deputies. In 2002, still as the PPS, it elected 15 federal deputies; in 2006 it peaked at 21. National president Alex Manente lost his bid for re-election to the Chamber from São Paulo, and former president Roberto Freire also failed in a race for a federal deputy seat. The only winner was GCM Romário Policarpo, elected state deputy in Goiás with 55,337 votes. Source: [oglobo.globo.com](https://oglobo.globo.com/blogs/lauro-jardim/post/2026/10/cidadania-caminha-para-desaparecer-do-mapa-politico-nacional.ghtml)

### Across the Region
**‘They take our water, our soil’: protesters fight ‘foreignisation’ as Javier Milei encourages land sales in Argentina: The Guardian**
The Guardian reports that President Javier Milei is courting billionaire investors by removing a block on foreign ownership of land and natural resources. On September 19, Marta Sahores, an 84-year-old chemistry professor, marched in Esquel, in Chubut province, during the marcha de la bronca. She held a sign defending the country’s water against what she called the government’s handover to investors; other signs read that the land is not for sale. Workers, retirees, students, Indigenous groups and human rights organisations marched with her. Sahores has mobilised against mega-mining projects for more than two decades. Source: [theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/global-development/2026/oct/06/argentina-land-reform-protests-javier-milei)

**A bola vai rolar no Brasileiro de futebol adaptado, em Niterói: O Globo**
Niterói hosts the 12th Brazilian power-soccer championship this Tuesday and Wednesday at the Associação Niteroiense dos Deficientes Físicos, in Rio do Ouro, with free entry, O Globo reports. Six teams take part: Clube Novo Ser, Rocinha Power Soccer, Rio de Janeiro Power Soccer, Minas Power Soccer, Fortaleza Power Soccer and Blue Angels. O Globo names as favorites Rio de Janeiro Power Soccer, Brazilian champion in 2025, and Clube Novo Ser, a four-time national champion and the first powerchair football team in Latin America. Four of eight players are on court at a time, the ball is 33 centimetres across, and the motorized chairs are limited to 10 kilometres an hour. Ricardo Gonzalez, director of Instituto Novo Ser, said the championship makes these athletes protagonists of a competition, a team and a sport; the discipline is seeking a place at the Los Angeles Paralympics in 2028. Source: [oglobo.globo.com](https://oglobo.globo.com/rio/bairros/niteroi/noticia/2026/10/06/a-bola-vai-rolar-no-brasileiro-de-futebol-adaptado-em-niteroi.ghtml)

### The Region and the World
**Revolução dos vinhos brancos; queda mundial do consumo; a safra espetacular de 2026: leia entrevista exclusiva com enólogo Sebastián Zuccardi: O Globo**
Sebastián Zuccardi, of the family winery in Mendoza’s Uco Valley, told O Globo in Rio de Janeiro — his first visit to the city — that he expects Argentina’s 2026 harvest to be memorable, a cooler year without excessive heat or rain, and that the first Zuccardi wine of that vintage should appear late this year or next year. He said Argentina is 4.8 percent of the world wine market, that about 80 percent of Argentine wine is drunk at home and 20 percent is exported, and that Brazil is one of the few countries where consumption is still growing, though tax makes wine expensive there. On a Mercosur–European Union agreement he said he does not know the detailed clauses, but he believes it would ease European wine into Latin America more than it would boost Argentine sales in Europe, and that market access is not equal if other producers receive subsidies. The family is building two wineries, one in the Uco Valley for Alambrado and one in Maipú for Santa Julia with a wine-tourism center, and he said they reinvest rather than take money out for personal use. Source: [oglobo.globo.com](https://oglobo.globo.com/blogs/saideira/post/2026/10/revolucao-dos-vinhos-brancos-queda-mundial-do-consumo-a-safra-espetacular-de-2026-leia-entrevista-exclusiva-com-enologo-sebastian-zuccardi.ghtml)

### Both Sides: Whether Uruguay should keep a president’s affinity with Lula apart from relations with Brazil
What is being decided is how Uruguay deals with Brazil after the October 25 presidential runoff, and the person drawing the line is President Yamandú Orsi.

Orsi’s case is that personal and party affinity must not write state policy. At a press conference on Monday he said that affinity, or what one knows of a person, cannot interfere in relations between countries. His best reason is continuity: he said his relationship with neighboring countries has been the same under one government or another, and that elections elsewhere have not, so far, pushed Uruguay to mix the two. He calls himself a personal friend of Lula and met him on September 21 in New York, during the UN General Assembly, where Orsi said they discussed trade, shared infrastructure, productive development, integration and regulation of sports betting. He said that friendship will not condition Uruguay’s stance if Flávio Bolsonaro is elected. His phrase was that one should not mix the matters up.

The other position is already public inside his own coalition. Infobae reports that the Frente Amplio, which Orsi belongs to, has explicitly backed Lula’s candidacy. So has the Movimiento de Participación Popular, the sector historically led by José Mujica, described there as an intimate friend of Lula. Several leaders of that sector were in Brazil, and Lucía Topolansky, Mujica’s widow, sent a message of support. Their stated act is an open political endorsement of Lula, not a neutral wait for the neighbor’s result.

Both are working from the same calendar: a second round on October 25, and a presidency in Montevideo that has already dealt with Lula as Brazil’s current president. Lula said he thanked Orsi for work so Brazil could take Uruguay’s beef-export quota to China, a step China did not accept. What happens next is that round. Orsi said Uruguay will see how to move according to the result that comes.

> **Falkland lawmakers may curb Argentine visitors after flag protests on the islands.**

**What You Need to Know:** Falkland Islands lawmakers are examining whether they can legally limit Argentine visitors after residents objected to flags and banners rejecting British sovereignty. Separately, Argentina’s cassation court has a 15 October hearing on rejoining two cases against Cristina Kirchner and Máximo Kirchner, and Sunday’s Brazilian count sent the presidency to a 25 October runoff.

### Lead
**Falklands weighs curbs on Argentine visitors after flag-waving incidents: MercoPress**
Residents of the Falkland Islands have been angered by Argentine visitors waving Argentine flags and banners denying British sovereignty, and members of the community are calling for such visits to be restricted. Argentine nationals can currently enter with a valid passport, proof of return travel, confirmed accommodation, health insurance and sufficient funds. Michael Goss, a Member of the Legislative Assembly, said he is personally not opposed to restrictions, but that “we can’t turn around and directly stop people coming in at this moment in time,” because it comes down to what can be done legally. He said the Assembly has already begun, at an early stage, to look at ways it might stop incidents of this kind, though that also depends on administration, and that people “visiting the Falkland Islands” to further a political agenda is “not acceptable.” Goss said the islands are hearing “a lot of noise” from Argentina, including sparks at the United Nations when he and Dom were away, but that “it’s just noise, and we’re not going to let it get to us.” MercoPress reports that such incidents have recurred as President Javier Milei’s government has stepped up Argentina’s sovereignty claim, including legal action against companies exploring for oil near the Islands. Source: [en.mercopress.com](https://en.mercopress.com/2026/10/05/falklands-weighs-curbs-on-argentine-visitors-after-flag-waving-incidents?utm_source=feed&utm_medium=rss&utm_content=main&utm_campaign=rss)

### Both Sides: Paving Praça do Pomar
Rio de Janeiro’s Barra subprefecture has begun rebuilding Praça do Pomar, in Jardim Oceânico, at a stated cost of 2.8 million reais, with completion expected in December. The question is how much of the square to pave, and the decision sits with the subprefecture after a letter from neighbours.

The strongest case for changing the plan comes from the residents’ association Amojo. Its president, Paulo Oighenstein, says a residents’ commission asked for less paving: keep part of the paths in saibro; on the main allée, lay concrete blocks on only one strip, with gaps for grass, and leave saibro on the rest; and pave toward the fountain only at gates that stay open, so wheelchairs and prams can pass. He says those changes, if made before the work is executed, would not raise the cost. Resident and lawyer Rogério Zouein says covering every path in concrete blocks will make the square hotter and harm its landscape, and that this runs against depaving programmes, including ones linked to Rio’s former environment secretary. An unnamed resident on the commission wants sand kept in the play space for children up to four, rather than the planned rubber floor, because she says the city does not maintain the sand.

The strongest case for going ahead comes from the subprefecture. It says that for years it received complaints that the soil is impassable on rainy days, and that residents asked for a pedestrian path and a draining surface. It says the tender followed a project approved after an earlier consultation, and that requests made later were sent to the technical area. It says no tree will be removed. The municipal conservation secretariat says damaged fence bars will be replaced and the existing fence repainted after sanding, cleaning, anti-corrosion paint and a finish coat. It says municipal decree 36,180 of 2012, which Zouein cites on work signs, covers private works and does not apply to public ones.

Architect and urbanist Vinicius Mattos, a UFRJ researcher, says the heat worry is justified if the mineralized area grows much, especially without shade. He also says hollow blocks with grass are a poor path surface, because grass fails under footsteps, compaction, shade and weak upkeep, and the ground can become uneven and less accessible. A paved path under trees, he says, can stay cooler than a so-called green surface in full sun.

Both sides accept that the rebuild is already under way and is scheduled to finish in December. The city says the later requests remain under technical review while demolition, new surfaces and the resetting of Portuguese stone continue. Source: [oglobo.globo.com](https://oglobo.globo.com/rio/bairros/barra/noticia/2026/10/05/obras-de-r-28-milhoes-em-praca-na-barra-geram-embate-entre-moradores-e-prefeitura.ghtml)

> **Thirteen Argentine governors want agreements, not Paris photos, on the twenty twenty-seven budget.**

**What You Need to Know:** Thirteen Argentine governors are pressing for agreements, not more Paris photographs, before they move on the twenty twenty-seven budget. Cabinet chief Diego Santilli is opening one-on-one talks on that budget, decree 70, and a political reform that would eliminate the PASO primaries. Brazilians are voting today in a first round polls still put short of an outright winner, and families of miners missing in Sinaloa are pressing a Canadian company over a pit, a mine, and 42,000 dollars.

# Omni View Central & South America

### Lead
**Tras la distención del clima en París, llegó el momento de transformar los gestos de los gobernadores en votos: La Nación**
After Argentina Week in Paris, Cabinet chief Diego Santilli is opening a new round of one-on-one contacts for agreements on decree 70, the 2027 budget, and a political reform that includes eliminating the PASO primaries, La Nación reports. President Javier Milei greeted each of the 13 governors who were there, thanked them for joining meetings with investors, and told them that appearing together was a good signal, in conversations of about 15 minutes, before they joined a photograph with Emmanuel Macron. Most of those 13 have decided to hold their provincial vote apart from the national election. What they are waiting to hear is how La Libertad Avanza will compete in their districts, with provincial elections in 2027 in view. Source: [lanacion.com.ar](https://www.lanacion.com.ar/politica/tras-la-distencion-del-clima-en-paris-llego-el-momento-de-transformar-los-gestos-de-los-gobernadores-nid04102026/)

### Across the Region
**Elecciones Brasil 2026, en vivo: la población acude a las urnas para votar entre dos modelos antagónicos de país: Infobae**
Brazilians are at the polls today in the presidential first round. The Defense Ministry has mobilized 26,500 service members from the Navy, Army, and Air Force for security and logistics in 482 municipalities across 12 states, covering 8,827 polling places, in an operation requested by the electoral courts and authorized by the presidency, Infobae reports. Voting is compulsory for citizens aged 18 to 70 and optional at 16 and 17. More than 158 million people are eligible; El País puts the figure at almost 159 million. Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, 80, of the Workers' Party, is seeking a fourth term and has said it would be his last. Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, 45, of the Liberal Party, is the main rival. Infobae counts Lula, Flávio Bolsonaro, and 11 other candidates; France 24 reports 12 names on the presidential ballot. Datafolha's latest survey, cited by WWBL, puts Lula at 42 percent and Bolsonaro at 38 percent, with a two-point margin of error. El País headlined a last poll at 45 percent to 42 percent. Infobae says the surveys do not project either man at the 50 percent required to win today; a runoff, if needed, is set for October 25. On Friday the United States closed its embassy in Brasília and its consulates after an alleged bomb threat; the Federal Police investigated and found nothing that confirmed the risk, La Nación reports. Lula's campaign asked the electoral courts to examine the episode as possible external interference and attributed the order to Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Donald Trump called the election "very important" for his country on Thursday and said on Friday he would follow it closely. El País reports that Jair Bolsonaro was convicted of leading a coup attempt; Infobae reports a 27-year sentence over the attempt that followed his 2022 defeat. Source: [infobae.com](https://www.infobae.com/america/america-latina/2026/10/04/en-vivo-elecciones-brasil-2026/) | https://elpais.com/america/2026-10-04/elecciones-en-brasil-2026-en-vivo.html | https://www.lanacion.com.ar/el-mundo/elecciones-en-brasil-2026-en-vivo-lula-vs-flavio-bolsonaro-y-las-ultimas-noticias-voto-a-voto-nid04102026/ | https://www.wwbl.com/2026/10/04/latin-americas-conservative-shift-faces-its-biggest-test-yet-in-brazil-election/ | https://www.france24.com/en/brazil-a-portrait-of-flavio-bolsonaro

### The Region and the World
**US Troops May Shift From Europe to the Americas, Hegseth Says: Kyiv Post**
Some U.S. units and capabilities now in Europe could move to the Western Hemisphere or back to the United States as Washington expands its military footprint in Central and South America, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said Saturday in Colorado Springs, the Kyiv Post reports. He tied that possibility to demands that European allies take on more of the burden of continental defense, under a posture review he said concludes in December. Hegseth said the United States is expanding its presence with partners and pointed to what he called the president's move in Venezuela, referring to the capture of former leader Nicolás Maduro. He named growing security cooperation with Ecuador, Honduras, Guatemala, and Panama, and said some capabilities could shift as the administration goes after groups it has designated terrorist organizations. Source: [kyivpost.com](https://www.kyivpost.com/post/86066)

### Both Sides: Whether governors should vote the 2027 budget and the political reform now
What is being decided is whether the governors who traveled to Paris should now supply votes for the 2027 budget, for decree 70, and for a political reform that includes eliminating the PASO primaries. Cabinet chief Diego Santilli is the official opening those talks.

The case for moving, as President Javier Milei put it to the governors before the meeting with Emmanuel Macron, is that they need to work together to avoid the return of kirchnerism, and that being seen together is a good signal after the investor meetings. Economy Minister Luis Caputo, at a shared dinner, described the provinces in the room as the ones the government wanted to reach agreements with because they had supported Milei's administration. According to La Nación, some sources said Karina Milei suggested that in those provinces the libertarians would not field heavyweight candidates — a remark the governors heard as a possible definition of how the national party would compete at home.

The case for waiting comes from the governors. Several told La Nación they have already given enough proofs of support, that the moment for agreements has arrived, and that there should be no more promises. Their calendar is the provincial elections of 2027, and what they say they still need is a clear account of how La Libertad Avanza will play in their districts. Most of the 13 have already decided to split that provincial vote from the national one.

# Omni View Central & South America
> **Three hundred fifty thousand dollars now buys Argentine citizenship for foreigners paying the treasury.**

**What You Need to Know:** Argentina’s government has unveiled a citizenship-by-investment programme: a non-refundable payment of 350,000 US dollars to the Treasury, or 800,000 US dollars in a seven-year bond, in exchange for an Argentine passport, with applications due to open before the end of the year. Across Brazil, O Globo finds that six of every ten reais in individual parliamentary amendments over three years went to the towns where those deputies took their largest local vote shares. In Costa Rica, fuel prices rose on Saturday, led by a 97-colón increase in diesel.

### Lead
**Argentina to sell citizenship to foreigners for US$350,000 to raise dollars: MercoPress**
Argentina’s government has unveiled a citizenship-by-investment programme that will let foreigners obtain an Argentine passport. One path is a non-refundable contribution of 350,000 US dollars to the Treasury. The other is the purchase of 800,000 US dollars in a seven-year government bond. MercoPress frames the programme as a way to raise dollars. Applications would open before the end of the year. Source: [en.mercopress.com](https://en.mercopress.com/2026/10/03/argentina-to-sell-citizenship-to-foreigners-for-us-350-000-to-raise-dollars?utm_source=feed&utm_medium=rss&utm_content=main&utm_campaign=rss)

### Across the Region
**Deputados destinam R$ 6 de cada R$ 10 em emendas para municípios onde tiveram melhor desempenho nas urnas: O Globo**
Of every ten reais federal deputies sent through individual amendments over the last three years, six went to cities where those deputies took the largest share of the local vote, an O Globo review finds. The 15 percent of municipalities with each lawmaker’s highest vote shares account for half of 43 billion reais in individual amendments directed since 2024. Adolfo Viana sent 4.9 million reais to Pojuca, Bahia, where he took 19.6 percent of valid votes for federal deputy in 2022, and nothing to neighboring Mata de São João, where his share was 0.32 percent. ### Both Sides: Alcohol sales on Brazil’s election day
Brazilians vote on Sunday, 4 October, and whether alcohol may be sold that day is decided state by state. The Superior Electoral Court sets no national ban. Regional electoral courts, working with public-security bodies, write the local rule, and state security secretariats may add limits of their own. A ban can cover a whole state or only some municipalities and electoral zones, and it can start the night before the vote.

The case for a restriction is the order those courts and security bodies have already signed where they chose one. They stop sale, supply, distribution and consumption, including delivery, for a fixed window around polling. Acre’s regional court set that ban from midnight to 16:00 on 4 October, and the same hours on 25 October if a runoff is held. Amapá runs from 22:30 on 3 October until 18:00 on 4 October. Alagoas suspends sales from 03:00 to 18:00. Amazonas runs from 02:00 to 17:00. Maranhão runs from midnight to 22:00. Pará and Piauí run from midnight to 18:00. In Bahia, 18 municipalities have adopted local hours that differ by electoral zone.

The case against a statewide ban is the choice of the three largest electorates, and a request from the trade. São Paulo, Minas Gerais and Rio de Janeiro will apply no alcohol restriction. São Paulo has had no dry law since 2006. Rio has not applied the measure since 1996. The Minas Gerais chapter of the Brazilian Bars and Restaurants Association asked the state government not to decree one. The Federal District, Espírito Santo, Paraná, Rio Grande do Sul, Mato Grosso do Sul, Paraíba, Pernambuco, Rio Grande do Norte, Rondônia and Santa Catarina also will not. Ceará and Roraima had not yet decided.

What both patterns accept is that there is no single national hour, and that Sunday’s vote goes ahead either way. Where a ban exists, it begins tonight or in the early hours of Sunday. Several of those orders repeat on 25 October if a second round is required. ### Both Sides: Destroying suspected trafficking boats off Ecuador
United States forces and Ecuadorian courts are now the actors in a fight over what may be done to crews stopped at sea. Between August 28 and September 16, 2026, Human Rights Watch said, US forces intercepted and destroyed eight Ecuadorian fishing vessels and detained more than 140 of 160 crew members. The case for the operations, as US forces stated it, is that the boats were floating refueling stations for drug trafficking linked to Los Choneros, an Ecuadorian criminal group. Juanita Goebertus, Americas director at Human Rights Watch, said intercepting fuel trafficking at sea may be an important step to stop criminal groups. The case against, which she put first as a limit on that purpose, is that the aim does not allow security forces to arrest people without evidence, destroy their vessels, or abuse them. Crew members she interviewed denied any illicit refueling role. Some reported beatings, threats meant to coerce confessions that they were trafficking fuel, and pressure to sign documents they could not understand. Of the 160 crew members, 90 face criminal investigations in Ecuador, judges ruled that the arrest of 56 was unlawful, and 14 were not brought before a judge. Neither government has publicly disclosed evidence linking individual crew members to a crime, Human Rights Watch said, and neither answered its request for comment. What both the US allegation and the crews’ denials sit on is that the vessels were intercepted and destroyed and that most of the crews were detained. Human Rights Watch said the sinking may have eliminated evidence of what the boats were doing, and it asked both governments to disclose the legal basis, the criteria for interception and destruction, and to investigate the reported abuses. About 31 percent of that sum went to companies in which the candidates are partners, and 69 percent went to relatives or family-linked businesses, including a wife, a brother-in-law, nephews and sons. Electoral law does not itself prohibit the hiring. Fernanda Lobo de Pinho, an electoral lawyer and member of the Brazilian Academy of Electoral and Political Law, says the test is whether the contract is real, necessary and at market rates, or whether campaign money could return to the candidate, with closer scrutiny when the Special Campaign Financing Fund or the party fund pays. ### Lead
**Accused drug lord known as "The Spider" extradited to California from Colombia: CBS News**
Colombian authorities flew Geovany Andres Rojas, known as Araña or The Spider, to California and placed him in the custody of federal agents, CBS News reports. He faces drug-trafficking and terrorism charges in the United States and had acted as a spokesman and leader of Comandos de la Frontera, a rebel group known for trafficking cocaine in Putumayo, on the borders with Ecuador and Peru. Rojas was arrested in Bogotá in February 2025; Colombia’s Supreme Court approved extradition in October, and former President Gustavo Petro then suspended it, arguing he needed Rojas for peace talks with rebel groups, including Comandos de la Frontera. Conservative President Abelardo de la Espriella, elected in June, lifted that ban and on Friday personally supervised the transfer, saying, “You don’t build peace by protecting narco-terrorists like this bandit,” and asking U.S. authorities that Rojas not negotiate deals that leave his crimes unpunished. U.S. Attorney Adam Gordon said Colombia and the Department of Justice were “making a clean sweep of narcoterrorists, starting with Araña.” De la Espriella has suspended talks with rebel groups; the iron-fist approach recently included militarizing a city in northern Colombia after a drug gang tried to impose a three-day curfew, and he has said he will work closely with the United States against drug trafficking. Colombia has struggled to contain rural violence as drug gangs and rebel groups fight over territory left by the FARC after the 2016 peace deal. ### Both Sides: When a school should expel a student
Ten days ago at unit two of Colégio Ícone, in Taquara, Rio de Janeiro, a physical-education teacher refereeing a football match marked a foul. Some students disagreed and physically attacked him. Police were called. The school suspended those involved, then a general council of the network decided they should not remain.

Fernando Venancio, the school’s maintainer and director-general, says three of the students had their enrollment locked, meaning they were expelled, under a scale — verbal and written warnings, suspensions, then closure of enrollment — explained when a student matriculates. He says the school suspended them at once, supported the teacher, reviewed the images, called a council, and summoned the families because they have a right to speak. The teacher is away and receiving the school’s support. The adolescents were summoned to testify at the thirty-second police station in Taquara, and the Guardianship Council is following the case. Venancio says the school will still, this year, review protocols for interclass games, hold a talk on competitiveness, and meet a representative of the Jacarepaguá-area Guardianship Council on school safety, relationships, and the consequences of acts.

Mônica Donetto Guedes, a psychoanalyst and parent guide, argues that violence is a limit that cannot be crossed or treated as normal, because settling conflict by force breaks the use of words. She distinguishes a fight between students, which she says the school should mediate, from an attack on a teacher, which she calls an attack on authority and on the rule. She argues that expulsion also shows the other students that aggression is not an accepted way to end a conflict, and that families have to help build limits.

Priscilla Montes, a specialist in neuroeducation and child development, argues that the productive question is which intervention protects the school community and still teaches, in proportion, not which punishment the student deserves. She says a bad act is not an identity, and that a purely punitive answer can deepen a student’s distance from school. She argues that a transfer does not end the school’s and the family’s responsibility, that schooling should continue, and that moving a student without a plan for the behavior can carry the problem somewhere else.

Natália Xavier, a pedagogue at Afya Unigranrio, argues that expulsion can be used when other strategies are not enough or when there is a concrete risk to the school community, and that a right to education is not tolerance of violence. She says the gravity has to be proved, and she lists serious physical assault, persistent threats, repeated bullying or cyberbullying, harassment, discrimination, carrying weapons, drug trafficking, or intentional destruction that puts people at risk. She says everyday indiscipline, low achievement, one-off conflicts, undone assignments, or family disagreements with the school do not justify expulsion, and that a student should not be punished for acts done only by the adults responsible for them.

Gabriel de Britto Silva, a lawyer, argues that expulsion must stay reasonable relative to the act, and that repeated disciplinary offenses, insubordination, disrespect of staff, and a serious insult can allow enrollment to be closed or not renewed only if the constitutional rights to a full defense and to answer the case are respected, under an administrative procedure based on an ethics code or the school’s internal rules.

The speakers accept that students physically attacked the teacher and that the school has to protect its community. Venancio’s next steps inside the school are the protocol review, the competitiveness talk, and the guardianship-council meeting, all still this year, while the police station and the Guardianship Council follow the case. Source: [oglobo.globo.com](https://oglobo.globo.com/rio/bairros/barra/noticia/2026/09/27/quando-expulsar-um-aluno-caso-de-professor-surrado-por-estudantes-reacende-debate-especialistas-avaliam.ghtml)

### Both Sides: How far schools should accelerate students with high abilities
How far public schools should move a student with high abilities is the question Brazil's new rules put in the classroom. Federal Law 15.436 of 2026, in force since June, created a national policy and a national registry and allows specialized support, an individualized plan, enrichment, and partial or full acceleration.

The case for moving faster is that a child who has already mastered the lesson gains nothing from repeating it. Bia Agra, who created the Coleção Horizontes in Guadalupe, built materials that compact what a child already knows so teaching can go deeper, and she says the materials do not replace the school. Priscila Melo says she started mothers' meetings in Maré because other families did not know where to begin; her son Álvaro, now 10, was measured at an IQ of 148.

The case against an IQ cutoff is just as direct. Cristina Delou, a psychologist who works in Méier, says there is no single IQ that defines giftedness, a test is a picture of one moment, and accelerating a child only because the score is above 130 is the biggest pedagogical error one can make. Her criterion is mastery of that stage's content plus a pedagogical assessment, and she says a student can stay in the class and advance in one subject. Bárbara Calmeto, of the Autonomia Instituto in Tijuca, says identification should ask what the child needs, not how intelligent the child is, and that a larger quantity of tasks is not enrichment.

Each side accepts that a good mark alone does not identify high ability, and that the federal law already includes enrichment beside acceleration. Next, Bill 2.799 of 2023, called Lei Alvinho, is scheduled for the Constitution and Justice Committee of Rio's state assembly on Tuesday, September 29.

**What You Need to Know:** Poverty in Argentina reached 32.3 percent of people in the first half of 2026, the National Institute of Statistics and Census reported, the first rise since the decline that began in mid-2024. Extreme poverty rose to 7.5 percent. In the 31 urban areas the household survey covers, 9,729,000 people were below the poverty line.

### Lead
**Poverty in Argentina rises to 32.3%, ending two years of decline: MercoPress**
Argentina’s National Institute of Statistics and Census reported on Thursday that poverty reached 32.3 percent of people in the first half of 2026, 4.1 points above the second half of 2025. That is the rise the government said yesterday would be published today, and it interrupts a downward path running since mid-2024. Extreme poverty rose 1.2 points, from 6.3 percent to 7.5 percent. In the 31 urban agglomerations of the Permanent Household Survey, 9,729,000 people were below the poverty line and 2,249,000 below the extreme poverty line; estimates published by Argentine media put the national figures at 15.4 to 15.5 million people in poverty and about 3.6 million in extreme poverty. In household terms, 24.4 percent fell below the poverty line and 5.6 percent below the extreme poverty line. Against the first half of 2025, when the rates were 31.6 percent and 6.9 percent, the increases are 0.7 and 0.6 points; the second-half 2025 reading of 28.2 percent had been the lowest since 2018, when the year closed at 27.3 percent. Poverty is measured by income against a basic basket: in June a family of four needed 1,531,473 pesos to stay above the poverty line and 689,853 pesos to avoid extreme poverty. Among children under 14, 44.5 percent live in households below the line, against 36.9 percent of those aged 15 to 29 and 28.8 percent of those aged 30 to 64. Concordia recorded 56.2 percent, Gran Resistencia 48.6 percent and Posadas 42.2 percent; surrounding districts of the Buenos Aires metropolitan area reached 36.9 percent against 11.1 percent in the City of Buenos Aires, and agglomerations of fewer than 500,000 people rose 4.9 points, against 3.9 points in larger centres. **‘Anatomy of State Cruelty’: UN report alleges deliberate and escalating rights abuses in Nicaragua: Latin America Reports**
The United Nations Group of Human Rights Experts on Nicaragua published a 47-page report on 21 September, titled “The anatomy of State cruelty,” denouncing a pattern of government repression, including disappearances and killings, over eight years. The dossier details 161 cases of enforced disappearance since April 2018, when protests over social security reforms widened into a national challenge to Daniel Ortega’s government and a violent crackdown left more than 300 people dead. Ortega and co-president Rosario Murillo recently suspended elections indefinitely, a step the account says has been criticized as cementing an effective dictatorship; the dossier splits the repression into four phases, from the 2018 Operation Clean-Up to post-2023 measures aimed at absolute control over state institutions and the population. ### Both Sides: A larger fall in the peso
What is in front of Argentina is not a statute signed today. It is advice to the government on the peso, set beside what a large foreign fund says it will do with its money.

**Brazil set to keep a R$2.12-a-litre diesel subsidy for 30 more days: O Globo**

### Both Sides: Anonymous accusations and platform orders
Argentina’s Supreme Court has ordered Facebook Argentina, the local unit of Meta, to delete anonymous Facebook and Instagram posts that called F.C., a regular student at the National University of La Plata’s Faculty of Humanities and Education, an “abuser,” and to turn over available data identifying the account holders. The order sets aside a ruling of the Federal Chamber of La Plata that had rejected his habeas data claim.

F.C.’s case, which the Court accepted, is that the campaign left him unable to defend himself. Posters with his face and the word “Abuser” went up across the faculty. Anonymous profiles, presented as linked to the faculty gender commission, accused him of imposing sex on his partner even when she objected, while he publicly backed feminism and abortion rights. He argued that a private matter that did not rise to public interest had been turned into a public shaming. The Court called it a kind of virtual escrache, said it put his honor and privacy at risk, and held that freedom of expression, including on the internet, is especially broadly protected but is not absolute and must be reconciled with honor, privacy, and the right to a defense. It told Facebook to remove the challenged URLs if they are still up.

The strongest case for leaving the posts in place is the one the La Plata chamber acted on when it rejected the claim, together with the weight the Supreme Court itself gave speech. The posts’ authors are not quoted in the reporting; what they published is the accusation, framed as a warning about someone they called a hypocrite. The chamber declined to order removal or identification. The Court did not treat the abuse allegation as a finding.

Both the student and the publishers of the posts are dealing with the same material: anonymous posts on Facebook and Instagram that used the word “abuser.” The Court and the chamber split on whether that required takedown and naming. > **Category 5 Hurricane Polo menaces Mexico's Pacific coast, with no landfall expected.**

**What You Need to Know:** Hurricane Polo is a Category 5 off Mexico's Pacific coast. Mexican authorities have warned of heavy rain, strong winds and dangerous surf, and the storm is not expected to make landfall. UN experts say Nicaragua's crackdown on opponents amounts to crimes against humanity, and Brazil is moving to bar candidates with suspected criminal ties from October's election.

### What This Show Covers
Listeners who want one region, every day, told straight, start here: Central and South America and the Caribbean, with what was decided, what happened, and what it changes and for whom. Each edition also holds one contested question, with the strongest case on each side, and one measurable sign of progress when the day's reporting has one.

The promise on geography is simple. This desk covers Mexico, Central America, the Caribbean islands and every country of South America. Mexico's domestic politics, economy and security belong here. A story from outside the region appears only for a concrete consequence inside it, and that consequence comes first.

The brief is read by Mira, the network's AI host. Stories are chosen and written by software from named newsrooms, and every item names its source. It will not take a side: every claim is attributed, and no party, government or people is praised or mocked.

Other Omni View desks and Omni View Top World News sit alongside this one.

Omni View Central and South America is part of the Nerra Network, an independent, ad-free network of shows at nerranetwork.com. If this is the region you want each morning, it is here.

### Lead
**Hurricane Polo strengthens to category 5 off Mexico's Pacific coast: Reuters**
Hurricane Polo has strengthened into a Category 5 storm off Mexico's Pacific coast and, in the Associated Press account, one of the strongest storms on record there. Mexican authorities have issued warnings as the storm threatens coastal areas with heavy rains, strong winds and dangerous surf. It is not expected to make landfall. ### Both Sides: Foreign action against organized crime
At the UN General Assembly, the question is how far governments outside a country should go in fighting organized crime in the region, and who decides. Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva told the assembly that Brazil needs cooperation, not intervention. He rejected any foreign role in combating organized crime. Reuters said the remarks were seen as directed at Washington and at domestic rivals. He also cautioned against outside interference in Brazil's October elections. The South China Morning Post reported that he told the United States Brazil is no one's backyard. The strongest case for that limit, as Lula stated it, is cooperation with Brazilian authorities rather than a foreign role he rejects, and an election free of outside interference.

The strongest case for going further, as officials have stated it, is the threat they name. The South China Morning Post reported that Secretary of State Marco Rubio defended US strikes on boats, warned of a drug-cartel "cancer," and pledged continued military operations against suspected drug traffickers in Latin American waters. The New York Times reported that 14 Latin American countries are expected, on the sidelines of the General Assembly, to designate 25 criminal groups as terrorist organizations, following the US lead, to enhance regional security cooperation.

What both accounts treat as given is that organized crime is a problem governments say they are responding to. The next dated marker Lula named is Brazil's October elections. The Times reported the designations as expected during this General Assembly.
